A long grey-white patch of old snow lies flat across the middle of the meadow, blue gentians blooming in a tight line exactly where its wet edge is melting back.
Every shaded gully between the rock ribs still holds snow packed hard and blue-grey, while the sunlit slope between them is buried in yellow and purple flowers.
A patch of old snow has been undercut into a hollow curved like a breaking wave, blue-shadowed inside where meltwater is running away beneath it and dissolving the floor.
A sheet of snow is pulling back from left to right across the picture, and the first centimetres of bright green following it are already studded with tiny white flowers.
A blue glacier tongue hangs above the flower line, its lower cliff dropping straight into shadow, its cracked blue face taller than anything growing below it.
A broad white snowfield fills the whole upper slope above the flowers from one side of the picture to the other, its lower edge sharp and clean against the colour below.
A bare grey rock peak stands straight out of the snowfield above, its faces too steep for snow to stick, dark stone rising into hard blue sky with nothing soft about it.
The forest ends in a ragged uneven edge far below like a tideline on a beach, the last few trees short and angled hard away from the prevailing wind.
A single stunted tree stands alone below the meadow, every branch growing from one side only, the windward side bare wood stripped clean and silver.
Three mountain ranges stand one behind the other across the full width of the picture, each one a paler blue than the one in front, all their ridgelines knife-edged in the thin air.
The valley floor is so far below that it dissolves into warm haze, while the orange hawkweed flowers at the bottom of the frame are individually sharp, every petal counted.
Cloud is pouring over a low notch between two peaks and spilling down the slope toward the flowers like cold water finding the lowest ground.
The meadow stands in hard direct sun above a flat white sea of cloud that has filled the valley to the brim, the tops of the nearest peaks floating above it like islands.
A torn cloud is dragging its shadow across the flowers from left to right, the shadow edge a clean diagonal between bright yellow and sudden grey-green.
Clear meltwater braids in three silver threads through the flowers, running roughly sideways across the picture, too cold and too fast to reflect anything but white sky.
A small still lake holds the doubled image of the peak above it, purple flowers growing right to the waterline on the near bank, bare broken rock on the far side.
Grey rock faces rise straight out of the flowers with no transition zone, the flowers growing right to the base of the cliff and the cliff offering them nothing back.
The meadow stops dead in a hard straight line where the bare rock plateau begins, the rock grey-orange and cracked, not a single plant crossing the border.
A long low ridge of pale broken rock runs across the picture, left over by a glacier that is gone, flowers covering only its sheltered downhill side, the windward face bare gravel.
Meltwater has carved a small channel straight through a flower patch, the exposed cut-bank showing black soil only two fingers deep before it hits solid cold gravel below.
Ice has pushed a band of shattered grey rock sideways across the upper meadow, the rock slabs tilted at odd angles, bright orange lichen the only colour on their faces.
A cluster of deep blue flowers is growing flat and tight against a boulder, pressed out of the wind into the gap between rock and ground, no stem standing higher than the loose stones around it.
Short stiff spikes of cream-coloured flowers grow in dense low clumps no higher than the rocks beside them, every clump angled slightly downhill by the weight of last winter's snow.
A small permanent snowbank is pressing a hard white edge against a cluster of red flowers, the flowers touching the snow, the snow not caring, both of them sharp and saturated.
Two ptarmigan stand motionless in their half-brown half-white spring plumage in the middle of the flower field, their coloring matching the patches of old snow still scattered around them.
